query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor quantity of tungsten (≈2 at%) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will improve its strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion stability by promoting nano‐scale precipitate formation along the lamellar interfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure as previously produced.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled microalloying addition of tungsten (≈2 at%) during alloy fabrication.
generation.conditions: Tested under cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep conditions), and in corrosive environments representative of aerospace service.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale tungsten-rich precipitates and/or tungsten-induced solid-solution strengthening localized at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten addition is expected to segregate at the lamellar interfaces, where it can reduce atomic diffusion and dislocation activity. This suppression of grain-boundary sliding and enhanced local cohesion is anticipated to yield a better balance between strength and ductility while reducing creep deformation and resisting corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Tungsten-doped alloys will exhibit statistically significant increases in tensile strength and ductility, lower room-temperature creep rates, and diminished corrosion currents compared to the undoped baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (strength, ductility, creep rate, and corrosion resistance) of the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy as reported in prior work.
generation.boundary: Results are anticipated to hold for alloys with similar eutectic lamellar structures when exposed to aerospace-relevant service conditions (extreme temperature cycling, sustained load, and corrosive environments).
generation.uncertainty: There is no direct prior evidence linking tungsten additions to interface stabilization in AlCoCrFeNi2.1, and the effectiveness of tungsten in forming the desired nano-precipitates under the specific processing conditions remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and (2) the same alloy with 2 at% tungsten addition. Process both under identical conditions ensuring a similar lamellar structure. Subject samples to cyclic thermal treatments, long-term tensile creep at room and elevated temperatures, and standardized corrosion tests in simulated aerospace environments.
measurements: Tensile strength and ductility via standard stress-strain tests
Room-temperature and elevated-temperature creep rates using constant load creep tests
Corrosion rates measured by electrochemical polarization (e.g., corrosion current density)
Microstructural analysis using TEM to detect tungsten-rich phases at lamellar interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% improvement in combined strength–ductility metrics, creep reduction, and lower corrosion rates) over the baseline alloy, or if no tungsten segregation or precipitate formation is observed at lamellar interfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.
